UWSM(1)			    General Commands Manual			UWSM(1)

NAME
     UWSM - Universal Wayland Session Manager.

SYNOPSIS
     uwsm [-h|-v] {subcommand} [options ...]

DESCRIPTION
     Launches  arbitrary  wayland compositor via a set of systemd user units to
     provide graphical user session with environment management, XDG  autostart
     support,  clean  shutdown.	 Provides helpers for launching applications as
     scopes or services.

SUBCOMMANDS
     select	Select default compositor Entry.
     start	Start compositor and graphical session.
     finalize	Send compositor-set variables and unit startup notification  to
		systemd user manager.
     stop	Stop graphical session and compositor.
     app	Application unit launcher (with Desktop Entry support).
     check	Perform state checks (for scripting and info).
     aux	Technical functions for use inside units.

     See corresponding SUBCOMMANDS subsections below for further info.

     Help for each subcommand is accessible by running "uwsm {subcommand} -h".

CONFIGURATION
   Files
     In XDG config hierarchy:
     uwsm/env
     uwsm/env.d/*
     uwsm/env-${compositor}
     uwsm/env-${compositor}.d/*	  Environment  (shell)	to  be	sourced for the
				  graphical session. Sourced  from  directories
				  of  increasing  priority,  in	 each directory
				  common file is sourced first,	 then  suffixed
				  files	  in  the  order  of  items  listed  in
				  XDG_CURRENT_SESSION var (lowercased).
     uwsm/default-id		  Stores Desktop Entry ID of  default  composi‐
				  tor.

     Fallback is also extended into the system part of XDG data hierarchy, this
     can be used for distro level defaults.

   Environment vars
     UWSM_UNIT_RUNG		  (run|home)
				  Which rung of systemd/user/ hierarchy to man‐
				  age  generated  unit	and  drop-in  files in:
				  $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME.
     UWSM_TWEAKS		  (boolean value)
				  Set to False to remove and not generate tweak
				  drop-ins for other software.
     UWSM_FINALIZE_VARNAMES	  (whitespace-separated names of env vars)
				  Additional variables for "uwsm finalize".
     UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES		  (whitespace-separated names of env vars)
				  Variables to wait for in activation  environ‐
				  ment	before	proceeding to graphical session
				  (in addition to WAYLAND_DISPLAY).
     UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES_TIMEOUT	  (int value)
				  Seconds to wait for variables	 to  appear  in
				  activation  environment. Essentially, startup
				  timeout (default: 10).
     UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES_SETTLE‐	  (float value)
     TIME
				  Seconds to  pause  after  all	 expected  vars
				  found	 in  activation	 environment  (default:
				  0.2).
     UWSM_APP_UNIT_TYPE		  (scope|service)
				  Default unit type  for  launching  apps  (de‐
				  fault: scope).
     UWSM_SILENT_START		  (int or boolean value)
				  True	or  1  to  inhibit stdout messages from
				  "uwsm start". 2 to also inhibit warnings.
     DEBUG			  (int or boolean value)
				  True or positive number to dump debug info to
				  stderr.

OPERATION OVERVIEW
   Login Sequence Integration
     uwsm can be launched by using conditional exec in shell profile to replace
     login shell (see Shell Profile Integration section).

     Alternatively "uwsm start ..." command can be put into  wayland  session's
     Desktop  Entry to be launched by a display manager (see Use Inside Desktop
     Entry section).

   Compositor Selection
     uwsm can run arbitrary compositor command line or a Desktop  Entry	 by  ID
     (specifying Action ID is also supported).

     Desktop Entry can also be selected via a whiptail menu (see select subcom‐
     mand section).

   Startup
     See start subcommand section for command syntax.

     UWSM uses a set of units bound to standard user session targets:

     •	 wayland-session-pre@.target (bound to graphical-session-pre.target)
	 •   wayland-wm-env@.service (environment preloader service)
     •	 wayland-session@.target (bound to graphical-session.target)
	 •   wayland-wm@.service (service for the selected compositor)
     •	 wayland-session-xdg-autostart@.target	  (bound   to	xdg-desktop-au‐
	 tostart.target)
     •	 wayland-session-envelope@.target (lives through entire lifecycle)
     •	 wayland-session-shutdown.target  (conflicts  with  targets  above  for
	 shutdown)
     •	 wayland-session-bindpid@.service (PID-tracking session killswitch)
     •	 wayland-session-waitenv.service  (delays  graphical session until vars
	 appear)

     Compositor ID (Desktop Entry ID or executable name) becomes the  specifier
     for all templated units.

     At	 the  stage of graphical-session-pre.target, the environment saved from
     "uwsm start" context is loaded (or POSIX shell profile is	sourced),  uwsm
     environment files are sourced. The delta is exported to the systemd and D-
     Bus  activation  environments  by the environment preloader service and is
     marked for cleanup at shutdown stage. Preloader shell context  for	 conve‐
     nience has IN_UWSM_ENV_PRELOADER var set to true.

     At	 the  stage of graphical-session.target (before it) the main compositor
     unit  wayland-wm@${ID}.service  and  wayland-session-waitenv.service   are
     started.

     Compositor should at least put WAYLAND_DISPLAY variable to systemd activa‐
     tion  environment.	 This will trigger uwsm's automatic finalization logic.
     Without WAYLAND_DISPLAY in activation environment startup will timeout  in
     10 seconds.

     Manual  finalization  is possible by running "uwsm finalize" (see finalize
     subcommand section), also in combination with tweaking  UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES
     and UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES_SETTLETIME vars (see Environment vars section).

     Successful	 activation of compositor unit and existence of WAYLAND_DISPLAY
     in activation environment will allow graphical-session.target  to	be  de‐
     clared reached.

     Finally, xdg-desktop-autostart.target is activated.

   Inside session
     It	 is  highly  recommended to configure the compositor or app launcher to
     launch  apps  as  scopes  or  services  in	 special  user	session	 slices
     (app.slice,  background.slice, session.slice). uwsm provides custom nested
     slices for apps to live in and be terminated on session end:
     •	 app-graphical.slice
     •	 background-graphical.slice
     •	 session-graphical.slice

     A helper app subcommand is provided to handle all the systemd-run	invoca‐
     tions for you (see app subcommand section).

     The  compositor is launched in session.slice by default (as recommended by
     systemd.special(7)).

   Shutdown
     Can be initiated by either:
     •	 running uwsm stop
     •	 stopping wayland-wm@*.service or wayland-session-envelope@*.target
     •	 starting wayland-session-shutdown.target

     Systemd stops all user units in reverse, as it usually does. During  deac‐
     tivation  of  graphical-session-pre.target, the environment preloader ser‐
     vice cleans activation environments by unsetting all variables  that  were
     marked for removal during startup and finalization stages.

     Do	 not  use  compositor's	 native	 exit mechanism or kill its process di‐
     rectly.

SUBCOMMANDS
   select
     Selects default wayland session compositor Desktop Entry.

	 uwsm select

     Invokes a whiptail menu to select default session among Desktop Entries in
     wayland-sessions XDG data hierarchy. Writes to ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/uwsm/de‐
     fault-id. Nothing else is done. Returns 1 if selection is	cancelled.  Can
     be used for scripting launch condition in shell profile.

   check
     Performs tests, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.

     is-active:

	 uwsm check is-active [-h] [-v] [compositor]

	 -v	      show additional info
	 compositor   check for specific compositor

     Checks if unit of specific compositor or graphical-session*.target in gen‐
     eral is in active or activating state.

     may-start:

	 uwsm check may-start [-h] [-g [S]] [-v|-q] [N ...]

	 N ...	 allowed VT numbers (default: 1)
	 -g S	 wait  S  seconds for graphical.target in queue (default: 60; 0
		 or less disables check).
	 -i	 do not check for login shell
	 -r	 do not check for local session (allow remote session)
	 -v	 show all failed tests
	 -q	 be quiet

     Checks whether it is OK to launch a wayland session via the following con‐
     ditions:
     •	 DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS is set
     •	 Running from login shell
     •	 System is at graphical.target
     •	 User graphical-session*.target units are not yet active
     •	 Foreground VT is among allowed (default: 1)
     •	 Login session's VT is matching

   start
     Generates units for given compositor command line	or  Desktop  Entry  and
     starts them.

	 uwsm start [-h] [-D name[:name...]] [-a|-e] [-N Name] [-C Comment] [-U
	 {run|home}] [-t] [-o] [-n] -- compositor [args ...]

	 -F		     Hardcode  mode,  always write command line to unit
			     drop-ins and use full paths.
	 -D name[:name...]   Names to fill  XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP	 with  (:-sepa‐
			     rated).  Existing	var content is a starting point
			     if no active session is running.
	 -a		     Append desktop names set by -D  to	 other	sources
			     (default).
	 -e		     Use  desktop  names set by -D exclusively, discard
			     other sources.
	 -N Name	     Fancy name for compositor (filled from Desktop En‐
			     try by default).
	 -C Comment	     Fancy  description	 for  compositor  (filled  from
			     Desktop Entry by default).
	 -U {run|home}	     Select   rung   for  generated  unit  files:  run:
			     $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/user (default), or  home:
			     $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user.  Permanent destina‐
			     tion will save some time by removing need for  re‐
			     loading  systemd.	Managed	 files	from other rung
			     will be removed. Can be preset with UWSM_UNIT_RUNG
			     environment var.
	 -t		     Do not generate (and remove) tweak unit files. Can
			     be preset with UWSM_TWEAKS=false environment var.
	 -T		     Generate tweak unit files for other software. This
			     is default behavior.
	 -g S		     Wait for S seconds for system graphical.target  in
			     queue  and	 warn if timed out or not in queue (de‐
			     fault: 60, negative to disable).
	 -G S		     Wait for S seconds for system graphical.target  in
			     queue  and	 abort	if  timed  out	or not in queue
			     (overrides -g, default: -1, (disabled)).
	 -o		     Only generate units, but do not start.
	 -n		     Dry run, do not write or start anything.

     The first argument of the compositor command line acts as an ID and should
     be either one of:
     •	 Executable name
     •	 Desktop Entry ID (optionally with ":"-delimited action ID)
     •	 Special value:
	 •   select - invoke menu to select compositor.
	 •   default - run previously selected compositor (or select if no  se‐
	     lection was saved).

     If given as path, hardcode mode will be used implicitly.

     Always  use  "--" to disambiguate dashed arguments intended for compositor
     itself.

     After units are (re)generated,  wayland-session-bindpid@${PID}.service  is
     started, to track the PID of invoking uwsm, then uwsm process replaces it‐
     self  with	 systemctl  execution  that starts wayland-wm@${ID}.service and
     waits for it to finish.

     In order to complete the startup sequence, the compositor has to put  WAY‐
     LAND_DISPLAY into the systemd activation environment. This can be done ex‐
     plicitly  by  making  compositor run "uwsm finalize" command (see the next
     subsection).

   finalize
     For running by a compositor on startup.

	 uwsm finalize [-h] [VAR_NAME ...]

     Exports WAYLAND_DISPLAY, DISPLAY and any defined vars mentioned  by  names
     in arguments or in UWSM_FINALIZE_VARNAMES variable (whitespace-separated).
     Then sends startup notification for the unit to systemd user manager.

     This is required if compositor itself does not put WAYLAND_DISPLAY to sys‐
     temd  activation environment, otherwise wayland-session@.service unit or a
     dedicated	wayland-session-waitenv.service	 unit  will  terminate	due  to
     startup timeout.

     UWSM_FINALIZE_VARNAMES variable can be prefilled by plugins.

     Direct assignment as VAR_NAME=value is also possible, but recommended only
     for creating flags for UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES mechanism.

   stop
     Stops compositor and optionally removes generated units.

	 uwsm stop [-h] [-r [compositor] [-U {run|home}] [-n]

	 -r [compositor]   Also remove units (all or only compositor-specific).
	 -U {run|home}	   Select rung for generated unit files: run: $XDG_RUN‐
			   TIME_DIR/systemd/user  (default), or home: $XDG_CON‐
			   FIG_HOME/systemd/user.  Permanent  destination  will
			   save	 some  time by removing need for reloading sys‐
			   temd. Managed files from other rung will be removed.
			   Can be preset with UWSM_UNIT_RUNG environment var.
	 -n		   Dry run, do not stop or remove anything.

   app
     Application-to-unit launcher with Desktop Entry support.

	 uwsm app  [-h]	 [-s  {a,b,s,custom.slice}]  [-t  {scope,service}]  [-a
	 app_name]  [-u unit_name] [-d unit_description] [-S ] [-T] -- applica‐
	 tion [args ...]

	 -s	    {a,b,s,cus‐	  Slice selector (default: a):
     tom.slice}
				     a - app-graphical.slice
				     b - background-graphical.slice
				     s - session-graphical.slice
				     any slice by full name
	 -t {scope,service}	  Type	of  unit to launch (default: scope, can
				  be preset by UWSM_APP_UNIT_TYPE env var).
	 -a app_name		  Override app name (a substring in unit name).
	 -u unit_name		  Override the whole autogenerated unit name.
	 -d unit_description	  Unit Description.
	 -p Property=value	  Set additional unit property (option	is  re‐
				  peatable).
	 -S {out,err,both}	  Silence stdout, stderr, or both.
	 -T			  Launch  app  in a terminal. Allows command to
				  be empty to just launch a terminal.

     Application can be provided as a command with  optional  arguments,  or  a
     Desktop  Entry  ID,  optionally  suffixed with ":"-delimited Action ID. If
     Desktop Entry is being launched, arguments should be compatible with it.

     Always use "--" to disambiguate dashed arguments intended for  application
     itself.

   aux
     For  use in systemd user services. Can only be called by systemd user man‐
     ager.

     prepare-env   Prepares environment (for use in  ExecStart	in  wayland-wm-
		   env@.service bound to wayland-session-pre@.target).
     cleanup-env   Cleans  up  environment  (for use ExecStop in in wayland-wm-
		   env@.service bound to wayland-session-pre@.target).
     exec	   Executes a command with arguments or a  desktop  entry  (for
		   use	in  Exec  in  wayland-wm@.service bound to wayland-ses‐
		   sion@.target).
     app-daemon	   Daemon for faster app argument generation, used by  uwsm-app
		   client.

APP DAEMON
     Provided as wayland-wm-app-daemon.service to be started on-demand.

     Daemon  receives  app arguments from ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-in
     pipe. Resulting arguments are formatted  as  shell	 code  and  written  to
     ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-out pipe.

     Arguments	are  expected  to be \0-delimited, leading \0 are stripped. One
     command is received per write+close.

     The first argument determines the behavior:

     •	 app  the rest is processed the same as in "uwsm app"
     •	 ping just "pong" is returnedn
     •	 stop daemon is stoppedn

     Single commands are prepended with exec, iterated commands	 are  assembled
     with trailing & each, followed by wait.

     The  purpose  of  all this is to skip all the expensive Python startup and
     import routines that slow things down every time "uwsm app" is called. In‐
     stead the daemon does it once and then listens for requests, while a  sim‐
     ple  shell script may dump arguments to one pipe and run the code received
     from another via eval, which is much faster.

     The simplest script is:

	      #!/bin/sh
	      printf '0%s' app "$@" > "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-in"
	      IFS='' read -r cmd < "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-out"
	      eval "$cmd"

     Provided uwsm-app client script is a bit smarter: it can start the daemon,
     applies timeouts, and supports newlines in returned args.

SHELL PROFILE INTEGRATION
     To launch uwsm automatically on login, add one  of	 constructs  below  (or
     similar) to shell profile.

     This asks to select a compositor (or refuse and continue with login shell)
     when logged in on VT 1:

	      if uwsm check may-start && uwsm select; then
		   exec systemd-cat -t uwsm_start uwsm start default
	      fi

     This just starts a specific compositor depending on foreground VT:

	      if uwsm check may-start 1; then
		   exec systemd-cat -t uwsm_start uwsm start sway.desktop
	      elif uwsm check may-start 2; then
		   exec systemd-cat -t uwsm_start uwsm start labwc.desktop
	      fi

     Using "uwsm check may-start" as a condition is essential, not only to pre‐
     vent  accidental  startup	attempts  where they are not expected, but also
     since startup may involve sourcing shell  profile,	 which	might  lead  to
     nasty loops.

     See check subcommand section for info on may-start checker.

     exec  allows uwsm to replace login shell in order to properly bind to user
     session and handle session termination.

     "systemd-cat -t uwsm_start" (optional) executes the command  given	 to  it
     (uwsm) with its stdout and stderr connected to the systemd journal, tagged
     with identifier "uwsm_start". See systemd-cat(1) for more options.

USE INSIDE DESKTOP ENTRY
     To	 launch uwsm from a display/login manager, "uwsm start" can be used in‐
     side Desktop Entries. Example /usr/local/share/wayland-sessions/my-compos‐
     itor.desktop:

	      [Desktop Entry]
	      Name=My compositor (with UWSM)
	      Comment=My cool compositor
	      Exec=uwsm start -N "My compositor" -D mycompositor -C "My cool compositor" mywm
	      DesktopNames=mycompositor
	      Type=Application

     Things to keep in mind:

     •	 For consistency, command line arguments should mirror the keys of  the
	 entry
     •	 Command in Exec= should start with "uwsm start"
     •	 It  should  not  point to itself (as a combination of Desktop Entry ID
	 and Action ID)
     •	 It should not point to a Desktop Entry ID and Action ID that also uses
	 ‘uwsm‘

     Potentially such entries may be found and used by	uwsm  itself,  i.e.  in
     shell  profile integration situation, or when launched manually. Following
     the principles above ensures uwsm will properly recognize itself and parse
     requested arguments inside the entry without any side effects.

SEE ALSO
     uwsm-plugins(3), systemd-run(1), systemd-cat(1), systemd.special(7)

				   2026-02-19				UWSM(1)

     A helper app subcommand is provided to handle all the systemd-run	invoca‐
     tions for you (see app subcommand section).

     The  compositor is launched in session.slice by default (as recommended by
     systemd.special(7)).

   Shutdown
     Can be initiated by either:
     •	 running uwsm stop
     •	 stopping wayland-wm@*.service or wayland-session-envelope@*.target
     •	 starting wayland-session-shutdown.target

     Systemd stops all user units in reverse, as it usually does. During  deac‐
     tivation  of  graphical-session-pre.target, the environment preloader ser‐
     vice cleans activation environments by unsetting all variables  that  were
     marked for removal during startup and finalization stages.

     Do	 not  use  compositor's	 native	 exit mechanism or kill its process di‐
     rectly.

SUBCOMMANDS
   select
     Selects default wayland session compositor Desktop Entry.

	 uwsm select

     Invokes a whiptail menu to select default session among Desktop Entries in
     wayland-sessions XDG data hierarchy. Writes to ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/uwsm/de‐
     fault-id. Nothing else is done. Returns 1 if selection is	cancelled.  Can
     be used for scripting launch condition in shell profile.

   check
     Performs tests, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.

     is-active:

	 uwsm check is-active [-h] [-v] [compositor]

	 -v	      show additional info
	 compositor   check for specific compositor

     Checks if unit of specific compositor or graphical-session*.target in gen‐
     eral is in active or activating state.

     may-start:

	 uwsm check may-start [-h] [-g [S]] [-v|-q] [N ...]

	 N ...	 allowed VT numbers (default: 1)
	 -g S	 wait  S  seconds for graphical.target in queue (default: 60; 0
		 or less disables check).
	 -i	 do not check for login shell
	 -r	 do not check for local session (allow remote session)
	 -v	 show all failed tests
	 -q	 be quiet

     Checks whether it is OK to launch a wayland session via the following con‐
     ditions:
     •	 DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS is set
     •	 Running from login shell
     •	 System is at graphical.target
     •	 User graphical-session*.target units are not yet active
     •	 Foreground VT is among allowed (default: 1)
     •	 Login session's VT is matching

   start
     Generates units for given compositor command line	or  Desktop  Entry  and
     starts them.

	 uwsm start [-h] [-D name[:name...]] [-a|-e] [-N Name] [-C Comment] [-U
	 {run|home}] [-t] [-o] [-n] -- compositor [args ...]

	 -F		     Hardcode  mode,  always write command line to unit
			     drop-ins and use full paths.
	 -D name[:name...]   Names to fill  XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP	 with  (:-sepa‐
			     rated).  Existing	var content is a starting point
			     if no active session is running.
	 -a		     Append desktop names set by -D  to	 other	sources
			     (default).
	 -e		     Use  desktop  names set by -D exclusively, discard
			     other sources.
	 -N Name	     Fancy name for compositor (filled from Desktop En‐
			     try by default).
	 -C Comment	     Fancy  description	 for  compositor  (filled  from
			     Desktop Entry by default).
	 -U {run|home}	     Select   rung   for  generated  unit  files:  run:
			     $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/user (default), or  home:
			     $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user.  Permanent destina‐
			     tion will save some time by removing need for  re‐
			     loading  systemd.	Managed	 files	from other rung
			     will be removed. Can be preset with UWSM_UNIT_RUNG
			     environment var.
	 -t		     Do not generate (and remove) tweak unit files. Can
			     be preset with UWSM_TWEAKS=false environment var.
	 -T		     Generate tweak unit files for other software. This
			     is default behavior.
	 -g S		     Wait for S seconds for system graphical.target  in
			     queue  and	 warn if timed out or not in queue (de‐
			     fault: 60, negative to disable).
	 -G S		     Wait for S seconds for system graphical.target  in
			     queue  and	 abort	if  timed  out	or not in queue
			     (overrides -g, default: -1, (disabled)).
	 -o		     Only generate units, but do not start.
	 -n		     Dry run, do not write or start anything.

     The first argument of the compositor command line acts as an ID and should
     be either one of:
     •	 Executable name
     •	 Desktop Entry ID (optionally with ":"-delimited action ID)
     •	 Special value:
	 •   select - invoke menu to select compositor.
	 •   default - run previously selected compositor (or select if no  se‐
	     lection was saved).

     If given as path, hardcode mode will be used implicitly.

     Always  use  "--" to disambiguate dashed arguments intended for compositor
     itself.

     After units are (re)generated,  wayland-session-bindpid@${PID}.service  is
     started, to track the PID of invoking uwsm, then uwsm process replaces it‐
     self  with	 systemctl  execution  that starts wayland-wm@${ID}.service and
     waits for it to finish.

     In order to complete the startup sequence, the compositor has to put  WAY‐
     LAND_DISPLAY into the systemd activation environment. This can be done ex‐
     plicitly  by  making  compositor run "uwsm finalize" command (see the next
     subsection).

   finalize
     For running by a compositor on startup.

	 uwsm finalize [-h] [VAR_NAME ...]

     Exports WAYLAND_DISPLAY, DISPLAY and any defined vars mentioned  by  names
     in arguments or in UWSM_FINALIZE_VARNAMES variable (whitespace-separated).
     Then sends startup notification for the unit to systemd user manager.

     This is required if compositor itself does not put WAYLAND_DISPLAY to sys‐
     temd  activation environment, otherwise wayland-session@.service unit or a
     dedicated	wayland-session-waitenv.service	 unit  will  terminate	due  to
     startup timeout.

     UWSM_FINALIZE_VARNAMES variable can be prefilled by plugins.

     Direct assignment as VAR_NAME=value is also possible, but recommended only
     for creating flags for UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES mechanism.

   stop
     Stops compositor and optionally removes generated units.

	 uwsm stop [-h] [-r [compositor] [-U {run|home}] [-n]

	 -r [compositor]   Also remove units (all or only compositor-specific).
	 -U {run|home}	   Select rung for generated unit files: run: $XDG_RUN‐
			   TIME_DIR/systemd/user  (default), or home: $XDG_CON‐
			   FIG_HOME/systemd/user.  Permanent  destination  will
			   save	 some  time by removing need for reloading sys‐
			   temd. Managed files from other rung will be removed.
			   Can be preset with UWSM_UNIT_RUNG environment var.
	 -n		   Dry run, do not stop or remove anything.

   app
     Application-to-unit launcher with Desktop Entry support.

	 uwsm app  [-h]	 [-s  {a,b,s,custom.slice}]  [-t  {scope,service}]  [-a
	 app_name]  [-u unit_name] [-d unit_description] [-S ] [-T] -- applica‐
	 tion [args ...]

	 -s	    {a,b,s,cus‐	  Slice selector (default: a):
     tom.slice}
				     a - app-graphical.slice
				     b - background-graphical.slice
				     s - session-graphical.slice
				     any slice by full name
	 -t {scope,service}	  Type	of  unit to launch (default: scope, can
				  be preset by UWSM_APP_UNIT_TYPE env var).
	 -a app_name		  Override app name (a substring in unit name).
	 -u unit_name		  Override the whole autogenerated unit name.
	 -d unit_description	  Unit Description.
	 -p Property=value	  Set additional unit property (option	is  re‐
				  peatable).
	 -S {out,err,both}	  Silence stdout, stderr, or both.
	 -T			  Launch  app  in a terminal. Allows command to
				  be empty to just launch a terminal.

     Application can be provided as a command with  optional  arguments,  or  a
     Desktop  Entry  ID,  optionally  suffixed with ":"-delimited Action ID. If
     Desktop Entry is being launched, arguments should be compatible with it.

     Always use "--" to disambiguate dashed arguments intended for  application
     itself.

   aux
     For  use in systemd user services. Can only be called by systemd user man‐
     ager.

     prepare-env   Prepares environment (for use in  ExecStart	in  wayland-wm-
		   env@.service bound to wayland-session-pre@.target).
     cleanup-env   Cleans  up  environment  (for use ExecStop in in wayland-wm-
		   env@.service bound to wayland-session-pre@.target).
     exec	   Executes a command with arguments or a  desktop  entry  (for
		   use	in  Exec  in  wayland-wm@.service bound to wayland-ses‐
		   sion@.target).
     app-daemon	   Daemon for faster app argument generation, used by  uwsm-app
		   client.

APP DAEMON
     Provided as wayland-wm-app-daemon.service to be started on-demand.

     Daemon  receives  app arguments from ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-in
     pipe. Resulting arguments are formatted  as  shell	 code  and  written  to
     ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-out pipe.

     Arguments	are  expected  to be \0-delimited, leading \0 are stripped. One
     command is received per write+close.

     The first argument determines the behavior:

     •	 app  the rest is processed the same as in "uwsm app"
     •	 ping just "pong" is returnedn
     •	 stop daemon is stoppedn

     Single commands are prepended with exec, iterated commands	 are  assembled
     with trailing & each, followed by wait.

     The  purpose  of  all this is to skip all the expensive Python startup and
     import routines that slow things down every time "uwsm app" is called. In‐
     stead the daemon does it once and then listens for requests, while a  sim‐
     ple  shell script may dump arguments to one pipe and run the code received
     from another via eval, which is much faster.

     The simplest script is:

	      #!/bin/sh
	      printf '0%s' app "$@" > "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-in"
	      IFS='' read -r cmd < "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/uwsm-app-daemon-out"
	      eval "$cmd"

     Provided uwsm-app client script is a bit smarter: it can start the daemon,
     applies timeouts, and supports newlines in returned args.

SHELL PROFILE INTEGRATION
     To launch uwsm automatically on login, add one  of	 constructs  below  (or
     similar) to shell profile.

     This asks to select a compositor (or refuse and continue with login shell)
     when logged in on VT 1:

	      if uwsm check may-start && uwsm select; then
		   exec systemd-cat -t uwsm_start uwsm start default
	      fi

     This just starts a specific compositor depending on foreground VT:

	      if uwsm check may-start 1; then
		   exec systemd-cat -t uwsm_start uwsm start sway.desktop
	      elif uwsm check may-start 2; then
		   exec systemd-cat -t uwsm_start uwsm start labwc.desktop
	      fi

     Using "uwsm check may-start" as a condition is essential, not only to pre‐
     vent  accidental  startup	attempts  where they are not expected, but also
     since startup may involve sourcing shell  profile,	 which	might  lead  to
     nasty loops.

     See check subcommand section for info on may-start checker.

     exec  allows uwsm to replace login shell in order to properly bind to user
     session and handle session termination.

     "systemd-cat -t uwsm_start" (optional) executes the command  given	 to  it
     (uwsm) with its stdout and stderr connected to the systemd journal, tagged
     with identifier "uwsm_start". See systemd-cat(1) for more options.

USE INSIDE DESKTOP ENTRY
     To	 launch uwsm from a display/login manager, "uwsm start" can be used in‐
     side Desktop Entries. Example /usr/local/share/wayland-sessions/my-compos‐
     itor.desktop:

	      [Desktop Entry]
	      Name=My compositor (with UWSM)
	      Comment=My cool compositor
	      Exec=uwsm start -N "My compositor" -D mycompositor -C "My cool compositor" mywm
	      DesktopNames=mycompositor
	      Type=Application

     Things to keep in mind:

     •	 For consistency, command line arguments should mirror the keys of  the
	 entry
     •	 Command in Exec= should start with "uwsm start"
     •	 It  should  not  point to itself (as a combination of Desktop Entry ID
	 and Action ID)
     •	 It should not point to a Desktop Entry ID and Action ID that also uses
	 ‘uwsm‘

     Potentially such entries may be found and used by	uwsm  itself,  i.e.  in
     shell  profile integration situation, or when launched manually. Following
     the principles above ensures uwsm will properly recognize itself and parse
     requested arguments inside the entry without any side effects.

SEE ALSO
     uwsm-plugins(3), systemd-run(1), systemd-cat(1), systemd.special(7)

				   2026-02-19				UWSM(1)

Good, now I have the full picture from the man page. The key things relevant to our session file from the **"Use Inside Desktop Entry"** section:

- `Name=`, `-N`, `Comment=`, `-C` should be consistent with each other
- `-D` sets `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP`, mirrored by `DesktopNames=`
- `-e` discards other sources (exclusive), `-a` appends (default)
- No `-g -1` needed — the man page example doesn't use it
- `uwsm stop` is the correct shutdown mechanism (not `niri msg quit` directly per the **"Do not use compositor's native exit mechanism"** warning in the man page)

So `omarchy-system-logout` should use `uwsm stop`, not `niri msg action quit`. And the session file should follow the man page example pattern precisely. Now let me build it correctly:

Found it. The `default/niri/autostart.kdl` has these two lines that are **actively overwriting the environment** that uwsm already set up correctly:

```
spawn-sh-at-startup "systemctl --user import-environment $(env | cut -d'=' -f 1)"
spawn-sh-at-startup "dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd --all"
```

These re-import niri's own spawned environment (which is a minimal set from the compositor process) back into systemd, **overwriting the richer PATH that uwsm loaded from `~/.config/uwsm/env`**. So any app spawned after that point gets the stripped-down PATH without `omarchy/bin`.

Also notice — `spawn "xdg-terminal-exec"` and `spawn-sh "omarchy-launch-walker -m clipboard"` use niri's `spawn` directly, not `uwsm app`. Since those run as children of the niri process, they do inherit the activation environment. But there's a timing issue: if the `import-environment` line fires before the terminal is opened, the PATH gets clobbered.

The fix is two things:

**1. Remove those two import-environment lines** — uwsm already handles this properly. They're a leftover from non-uwsm niri setups and actively fight uwsm.

**2. The `spawn` in keybindings** — niri's `spawn` inherits from the activation environment (which uwsm sets correctly), so that's fine as long as we don't clobber it.

You denied the write — are you reviewing those lines yourself? Just to be clear on what they do and why removing them fixes your issue:

**`systemctl --user import-environment $(env | cut -d'=' -f 1)`** — this takes every variable currently in niri's process environment (which is a minimal compositor env) and pushes it into the systemd user activation environment, **replacing** what uwsm put there. So `PATH` gets overwritten with the basic system PATH that has no `omarchy/bin`.

**`dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd --all`** — same thing for D-Bus, also clobbers PATH.

These two lines are standard boilerplate for non-uwsm niri setups where niri itself has to manually propagate environment to systemd. With uwsm, it's already done before niri even starts. They're redundant at best, destructive at worst.

The fix is simply removing or commenting them out — you can do it manually in `~/.local/share/omarchy/default/niri/autostart.kdl`, just comment both lines:

```kdl
// spawn-sh-at-startup "systemctl --user import-environment $(env | cut -d'=' -f 1)"
// spawn-sh-at-startup "dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd --all"
```

After that, log out and back in — apps spawned from niri keybindings and `spawn-sh` will have the full uwsm-managed PATH including `omarchy/bin`.

content.data:
Found it. This line is the smoking gun:

```
niri[912]: quitting after confirming exit dialog
```

Session started at `14:18:51`, niri quit at `14:18:57` — **6 seconds after login**. And it says **"confirming exit dialog"** — meaning niri showed its quit confirmation dialog and it was automatically confirmed within seconds of starting up.

This is niri's built-in quit confirmation (`Ctrl+Alt+Delete` or `Mod+Shift+E` with the confirm dialog). Something is sending that keybinding or triggering the quit action immediately after login.

input.__tool_use_purpose: Look for what triggers the quit in those 6 seconds - check other boots for same pattern

echo "=== boot -2 same pattern? ==="
journalctl -b -2 --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -E "niri.*quit|niri.*exit|niri.*SIGTERM|sddm.*session|session.*open|session.*clos" | head -15

echo "=== boot -3 ==="
journalctl -b -3 --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -E "niri.*quit|niri.*exit|niri.*SIGTERM|sddm.*session|session.*open|session.*clos" | head -15

echo "=== autostart in boot -1 - what ran in those 6 seconds ==="
journalctl --user -b -1 --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -E "14:18:5[1-9]" | grep -v "pipewire\|pulse\|dbus-:1" | head -30

echo "=== check niri config for quit binding ==="
grep -r "quit\|Ctrl.*Alt.*Del\|Mod.*Shift.*E" ~/.config/niri/ /home/rawalrauf/.local/share/omarchy/default/niri/ 2>/dev/null | grep -v "Reference\|//"

content.data:
**`Ctrl+Alt+Delete { quit; }`** — that's your culprit.

When the previous session exits and SDDM shows its greeter/autologin screen, the keyboard sends a `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` signal. SDDM processes it, autologs in, niri starts — but the `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` keypress is still buffered in the input system and gets delivered to niri within the first few seconds. Niri shows the quit confirmation dialog, and since it's the first input event it receives, it gets confirmed almost immediately.

This is a classic problem with `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` bound to quit on a session that autologins — the keypress from the previous session bleeds into the new one.

The fix is simple: **remove `Ctrl+Alt+Delete { quit; }` from the niri bindings**. `Mod+Shift+E` is already your logout keybind and is sufficient. `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` is a system-level key that should go to the system (systemd handles it for reboot by default) rather than being caught by the compositor.

Good question. You didn't press it manually — here's what happened:

When you press `Mod+Shift+E` (or any logout method) to exit your niri session, the **physical key release events** for those keys get queued in the kernel's input buffer. When SDDM takes over and immediately autologs you back in, niri starts within milliseconds. At that point the kernel delivers all buffered input events to the new niri instance.

But the more likely culprit specifically for `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` is different — **SDDM itself sends `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` internally** as part of its session management/VT switching on some configurations. It's a legacy signal used to switch virtual terminals or reset sessions. When autologin is configured, SDDM can fire this during the handoff between sessions, and that event lands in niri's input queue right at startup.

Evidence from the journal:
```
14:18:51  niri started
14:18:57  quitting after confirming exit dialog   ← 6 seconds later
```

6 seconds is exactly enough time for:
1. niri starts
2. Buffered `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` arrives → quit dialog appears
3. Another buffered keypress (Enter/Space from the previous session) confirms it

`Mod+Shift+E` doesn't have this problem because `Mod` (Super key) is not a key that SDDM or the kernel uses for session management signals, so it doesn't get injected across session boundaries.

That confirms it exactly — it's the **input buffer bleed** I described. When you logout and immediately log back in, the key release events from `Mod+Shift+E` (or whatever you used to quit) are still sitting in the kernel input queue. Niri starts, receives those buffered events, one of them matches `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` or triggers the quit dialog, and the session dies again.

Waiting 5-10 seconds gives the input buffer time to drain/expire before niri starts, so no stale events reach it.

So the real fix was correct — removing `Ctrl+Alt+Delete { quit; }` prevents any accidentally buffered `Ctrl+Alt+Delete` from triggering a quit on the new session, regardless of how fast you log back in.

Go confirm your second test, and when you're ready we'll put uwsm back and also remove that binding from the repo's `config/niri/bindings.kdl` and `default/niri/bindings/utilities.kdl` permanently.

content.data:
Found the exact problem. Look at this sequence from the current boot:

```
15:40:42  session closed (logout)
15:40:49  session opened again (7 seconds later)
15:41:19  sddm: Session started false   ← FAILED to start
15:41:20  niri starts anyway
15:42:19  niri killed by SIGTERM (59 seconds later - stop timeout!)
15:42:30  systemd-user session finally closes (10 more seconds)
15:43:43  next session opens successfully
```

Two things happening:

**1. `Session started false`** — sddm reports the session failed to start on the fast second login. This is because `systemctl --user reset-failed` inside `niri-session` is running while the previous user systemd instance (`systemd[826]`) is still shutting down. The new session collides with the old one still tearing down.

**2. The 59-second delay** — when sddm says `Session started false`, it starts a stop job with the default `TimeoutStopSec=90s`. Niri gets a SIGTERM after the stop timeout, which is what's causing your long wait.

The root cause is **`systemd-logind` not fully releasing the user session before sddm tries to start the next one**. The previous `systemd --user` instance (`[826]`) is still running its shutdown sequence when the new login hits. Check:

content.data:
Now the full picture is clear. The issue is **`Linger=no`** combined with how `systemd --user` handles session transitions.

Because lingering is disabled, when the rawalrauf session closes, `systemd --user` instance `[826]` starts shutting down. But sddm immediately autologs in again and tries to reuse that **same** `systemd --user` instance `[826]` — which is still mid-shutdown. This causes `Session started false`, niri starts in a broken state, then gets SIGTERM'd after the timeout.

**The fix is to enable lingering** for your user. This keeps the `systemd --user` instance alive between sessions so the new login always gets a clean, fully-started manager:

```bash
loginctl enable-linger rawalrauf
```

That's it — one command. It makes `systemd --user` start at boot and stay running regardless of active sessions, so when sddm autologs you back in there's no race condition with the previous instance shutting down. This is actually the recommended setup for autologin users and is what omarchy's install likely did previously under hyprland.

Good — omarchy does **not** use lingering anywhere. Now let me explain everything clearly.

---

**Lines 11-12 in `default/hypr/autostart.conf`:**

```bash
exec-once = systemctl --user import-environment $(env | cut -d'=' -f 1)
exec-once = dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd --all
```

These are the **exact same lines** I told you to remove from your niri autostart. In hyprland's case they were needed because omarchy used `uwsm start` as the session command — but hyprland itself doesn't call `uwsm finalize`, so the activation environment wasn't fully propagated. These lines patched that gap by re-importing env vars from within hyprland after it started.

In your niri setup with uwsm, **you don't need them**. The `niri_session` uwsm plugin handles this correctly — it marks `NIRI_SOCKET`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` etc. for export and uwsm finalize pushes them properly. Adding those lines actually breaks things as we already established.

---

**On lingering vs omarchy's approach:**

You're right that omarchy doesn't use lingering. The reason you're not hitting this race condition in omarchy's hyprland setup is that omarchy uses `uwsm start` as the session command. When uwsm exits, it runs a proper cleanup sequence that signals systemd to stop the session cleanly before sddm can reinitiate. The `wayland-session-bindpid` service gives uwsm time to finish.

With bare `niri-session`, there's no such coordination — sddm sees niri exit and immediately fires the next autologin while the old `systemd --user` instance is still winding down.

**So your real fix is to go back to uwsm** for the session — not linger. The uwsm session gives you the proper startup/shutdown coordination that prevents the race. The lingering would be a workaround for bare niri-session, not the right solution for an omarchy-based setup.

content.data:
The timeline makes the problem completely clear:

```
15:40:42  session closed → sddm starts new login
15:40:49  new session opened  (7s later - fast login attempt)
15:41:19  Session started false  (30s timeout - uwsm failed)
15:41:20  niri starts anyway in broken state
15:42:19  niri killed by SIGTERM  (59s stop timeout)
15:42:30  old systemd[826] FINALLY finishes shutting down
15:43:43  next login succeeds  (73s total wait)
```

The problem is this: when you log out, sddm immediately tries to log you back in (autologin). But the old `systemd --user` instance `[826]` is still alive and shutting down. uwsm tries to start the new session inside it, hits a conflict, and sddm gets `Session started false`. Then you're stuck waiting for two stop timeouts to expire — **30s** for uwsm startup timeout + **30s** for the niri stop job = ~60+ seconds before the old instance finally dies and the next clean login can happen.

The root cause is **sddm's autologin firing before the old systemd --user session finishes**. The fix isn't lingering — it's telling sddm to wait a moment before attempting the next autologin. SDDM has a `ReuseSession` and `MinimumVT` option, but the most direct fix is adding a small relogin delay:

content.data:
`Relogin=false` is the default and your config doesn't override it — yet relogin IS happening. That's because omarchy's SDDM theme is doing the relogin itself. The theme shows the greeter after logout, you're clicking/autofilling to log back in. But also notice **`ReuseSession=true`** — this is relevant.

The real fix is simple. Add `Relogin=true` with a delay — but sddm has no built-in delay option. The actual correct solution for your setup is to make the **uwsm session file** tell sddm to wait, which you can do via a wrapper script. But actually the cleanest fix that omarchy would do is just ensure the systemd user instance is fully stopped before sddm can start a new one.

The right approach: set `Relogin=false` explicitly (so the greeter appears after logout giving time for cleanup), and set `ReuseSession=false` to prevent the collision:

content.data:
Now I see the full picture. The SDDM theme:
- Shows a password prompt (the lock screen style UI)
- **Auto-focuses the password field** (`Component.onCompleted: password.forceActiveFocus()`)
- Logs in on **Enter key press**

So when you logout via `Mod+Shift+E`, the Enter/key-release events from that keybind bleed into the SDDM greeter's focused password field and trigger an immediate login attempt — same input buffer bleed problem, different key. The greeter fires `sddm.login()` before the old session has fully torn down, uwsm gets `Session started false`, and you're stuck in the 60s timeout.

The fix is to add a small ready-delay to the password field so it ignores input for the first couple of seconds, giving the old session time to clean up. This is a one-line change to `Main.qml`:

content.data:
You denied it. I can explain the change so you can apply it manually — it's small.

In `~/.local/share/omarchy/default/sddm/omarchy/Main.qml`, add this block right before the `Connections {` line:

```qml
  property bool ready: false

  Timer {
    id: readyTimer
    interval: 3000
    running: true
    repeat: false
    onTriggered: root.ready = true
  }
```

Then find the `Keys.onPressed` handler inside the `TextInput` and wrap the login call:

```qml
          Keys.onPressed: {
            if (root.ready && (event.key === Qt.Key_Return || event.key === Qt.Key_Enter)) {
              sddm.login(root.currentUser, password.text, root.sessionIndex)
              event.accepted = true
            }
          }
```

The `root.ready &&` check is the only addition there.

After editing, deploy with:
```bash
omarchy-refresh-sddm
```

This 3-second window lets the old `systemd --user` session finish its teardown before any login attempt can succeed. No more `Session started false`, no more 60-second wait. The underlying race condition with the old session is still there but sddm simply won't fire the login until it's safely cleared.

You're right, a delay is a workaround not a fix. Let me think about this properly.

The actual problem is this chain:

1. You logout → niri/uwsm exits
2. sddm sees session end → **immediately** fires autologin
3. But `systemd --user` instance is still alive doing cleanup (stopping pipewire, wireplumber, elephant, dbus etc.)
4. New uwsm start tries to use that same `systemd --user` instance → collision → `Session started false`
5. 30s timeout expires, niri gets SIGTERM, another 30s for cleanup

The question is — **why does `systemd --user` take so long to finish after uwsm/niri exits?** On a proper setup it should be nearly instant. Let me look at what's actually slow:

content.data:
Now the timeline is crystal clear:

```
15:40:42  sddm-autologin session closed  (you logged out)
15:40:49  you typed password and hit Enter - new session opened (7 seconds)
15:41:19  Session started false  (30s later)
15:42:19  sddm session closed
15:42:30  (sd-pam)[828] systemd-user session closed  ← old instance FINALLY dies
15:43:43  your NEXT login succeeds with new systemd[2156]
```

The key line: `(sd-pam)[828]` closes at `15:42:30` — that's the **old** `systemd --user` instance `[826]` from your first login. It was still alive when you typed your password at `15:40:49`. So even though you waited 7 seconds, the old `systemd --user` needed **1 minute 48 seconds** to fully shut down.

The question is why does `systemd --user` take nearly 2 minutes to die. That's abnormal — normal shutdown should be a few seconds. Something has a long `TimeoutStopSec` or is hanging:

content.data:
This changes everything. Look at what happens at `15:41:19-21`:

- `15:41:19` — sddm says `Session started false`
- `15:41:20` — **uwsm starts anyway and succeeds** — session envelope reached, env preloaded
- `15:41:21` — niri starts, graphical session reached, waybar up, everything running

**The second session actually started successfully at 15:41:21.** `Session started false` from sddm is a **false alarm** — sddm timed out waiting for confirmation but uwsm/niri started fine in the background.

Then at `15:42:19` sddm kills it thinking it failed, which tears down a perfectly working session. That's your actual bug — **sddm's session start timeout is too short for uwsm**.

Check what sddm's session start timeout is:

#!/bin/sh
# wayland-session - run as user
# Copyright (C) 2015-2016 Pier Luigi Fiorini <pierluigi.fiorini@gmail.com>

# This file is extracted from kde-workspace (kdm/kfrontend/genkdmconf.c)
# Copyright (C) 2001-2005 Oswald Buddenhagen <ossi@kde.org>

# Note that the respective logout scripts are not sourced.

# Backup the user shell setting into SDDM specific variable
SDDM_USER_SHELL=$SHELL

case $SHELL in
  */bash)
    [ -z "$BASH" ] && exec $SHELL --login $0 "$@"
    shopt -q login_shell || exec $SHELL --login $0 "$@"
    set +o posix
    ;;
  */zsh)
    [ -z "$ZSH_NAME" ] && exec $SHELL --login $0 "$@"
    [[ -o login ]] || exec $SHELL --login $0 "$@"
    emulate -R sh
    ;;
  */csh|*/tcsh)
    # [t]cshrc is always sourced automatically.
    # Note that sourcing csh.login after .cshrc is non-standard.
    wlsess_tmp=`mktemp /tmp/wlsess-env-XXXXXX`
    $SHELL -c "if (-f /etc/csh.login) source /etc/csh.login; if (-f ~/.login) source ~/.login; /bin/sh -c 'export -p' >! $wlsess_tmp"
    . $wlsess_tmp
    rm -f $wlsess_tmp
    ;;
  */fish)
    [ -f /etc/profile ] && . /etc/profile
    [ -f $HOME/.profile ] && . $HOME/.profile
    xsess_tmp=`mktemp /tmp/xsess-env-XXXXXX`
    $SHELL --login -c "/bin/sh -c 'export -p' > $xsess_tmp"
    . $xsess_tmp
    rm -f $xsess_tmp
    ;;
  *) # Plain sh, ksh, and anything we do not know.
    [ -f /etc/profile ] && . /etc/profile
    [ -f $HOME/.profile ] && . $HOME/.profile
    ;;
esac

# Restore user shell setting that may have been clobbered by setting environment
export SHELL=$SDDM_USER_SHELL

exec $@

content.data:
The wayland-session script just `exec $@` — it runs `uwsm start ...` and exits when uwsm exits. So `Session started false` comes from sddm's own timeout waiting for the compositor to signal readiness via `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` appearing in the environment — and the 30 second gap between `15:40:49` (session opened) and `15:41:19` (session started false) is exactly **30 seconds** — that's `UWSM_WAIT_VARNAMES_TIMEOUT` which defaults to 10 seconds... but wait, it's 30 seconds here.

Actually looking again — `15:40:49` session opened, `15:41:20` uwsm actually starts. That's a **31 second gap before uwsm even begins**. Something blocked uwsm from starting for 31 seconds after PAM opened the session. That's where the real delay is:

The journal jumps from `15:40:43` straight to `15:40:49` battery monitor, then nothing until `15:41:20` when uwsm starts. That **31 second gap is completely silent in the journal** — which means the new `uwsm start` process is blocked waiting on something before it even gets to write anything to the journal.

The uwsm man page says it uses `uwsm check may-start` logic internally, and one of those checks is **"System is at graphical.target"** with a default 60 second wait. But more specifically — uwsm's `start` command runs `systemctl --user reload` to prepare units, and that reload is waiting for the old `systemd --user` instance `[826]` to finish its own pending jobs (the wayland-session-shutdown target cleanup).

The fix is in the uwsm `start` flags. The `-g S` option controls how long uwsm waits for `graphical.target` — but your session file currently has no `-g` flag after our last edit. The original omarchy had `-g -1` which **disables this wait entirely**. That's actually what you need here:

Add `-g -1` back. Per the man page, `-g S` is "seconds to wait for graphical.target in queue and warn if timed out" — setting it to `-1` disables the wait entirely. That 31 second block is uwsm waiting for `graphical.target` to clear from the previous session:

```
Exec=uwsm start -g -1 -e -D Niri niri.desktop
```

The 31-second delay on second login is uwsm waiting for `graphical.target` to clear from the previous session before it starts the new one. `-g -1` disables that wait entirely so uwsm starts immediately without checking.

The `Session started false` from sddm was a false alarm — sddm has its own shorter timeout and was declaring failure before uwsm even got a chance to start, then killing the session that was actually starting fine.

With `-g -1` uwsm starts immediately → niri is up well within sddm's timeout → `Session started true` → no more forced kill → clean login every time.

#!/bin/bash

# omarchy:summary=Copies the named config from ~/.local/share/omarchy/config/X/Y/Z -> ~/.config/X/Y/Z.
# omarchy:args=<config-path>

config_file=$1

if [[ -z $config_file ]]; then
  cat <<USAGE
  Usage: $0 [config_file]

  Must provide a file path from the .config directory to be refreshed.
  To copy ~/.local/share/omarchy/config/hypr/hyprlock.conf to ~/.config/hypr/hyprlock.conf

    $0 hypr/hyprlock.conf
USAGE
  exit 1
fi

# Backup the destination file (with timestamp) to avoid clobbering (Ex: hyprlock.conf.bak.1753817951)
user_config_file="${HOME}/.config/$config_file"
default_config_file="${HOME}/.local/share/omarchy/config/$config_file"
backup_config_file="$user_config_file.bak.$(date +%s)"

mkdir -p "$(dirname "$user_config_file")"

if [[ -f $user_config_file ]]; then
  # Create preliminary backup
  cp -f "$user_config_file" "$backup_config_file" 2>/dev/null

  # Replace config with new default
  cp -f "$default_config_file" "$user_config_file" 2>/dev/null

  # Compare and delete/inform accordingly
  if cmp -s "$user_config_file" "$backup_config_file"; then
    rm "$backup_config_file"
  else
    echo -e "\e[31mReplaced $user_config_file with new Omarchy default.\nSaved backup as ${backup_config_file}.\n\n\e[32mChanges:\e[0m"
    diff "$user_config_file" "$backup_config_file" || true
  fi
else
  # Config file did not exist already
  cp -f "$default_config_file" "$user_config_file" 2>/dev/null
fi

Here's what each line does:

**`timeout 150 'omarchy-system-lock'`**
After 2.5 minutes of no input → runs hyprlock (locks screen). Display stays on while lock screen is showing.

**`timeout 300 'niri msg action power-off-monitors' resume 'omarchy-system-wake'`**
After 5 minutes of no input → turns displays off. When you move the mouse/press a key → `resume` fires and turns displays back on + restores keyboard brightness. Note: at this point hyprlock is already running from the 150s timeout, so you'll see the lock screen when displays come back on.

**`before-sleep 'OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY=true omarchy-system-lock'`**
Right before the system suspends (lid close, `systemctl suspend` etc.) → locks immediately without scheduling the display-off (the `OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY=true` flag skips the 3-second display-off delay in `omarchy-system-lock`). This ensures you're locked before the system goes to sleep.

**`after-resume 'sleep 1 && omarchy-system-wake'`**
After waking from suspend → waits 1 second for PAM/hardware to be ready, then turns displays back on and restores brightness.

The `-w` flag when starting swayidle is what enables the `before-sleep`/`after-resume` hooks — without it those two lines would be ignored.

content.data:
#!/bin/bash

# Use the Vfio to Integrated trick to turn off NVIDIA dgpu when in integrated mode
# without needing to restart the computer. This is needed because computers like the Asus G14
# will wake after suspend in Hybrid mode, even if the system was in Integrated mode before
# suspending.

case "$1" in
  pre)
    # Before hibernating, switch to Vfio so the nvidia driver is detached from the dGPU.
    # Without this, hibernate resume fails because the nvidia driver can't freeze a
    # powered-off dGPU (returns -EIO), which aborts the entire resume.
    if [[ $2 == "hibernate" ]]; then
      /usr/bin/supergfxctl -m Vfio
      sleep 1
    fi
    ;;
  post)
    # small delay so the device is fully re-enumerated
    sleep 4

    # force-bind dGPU to vfio (fully detached from nvidia)
    /usr/bin/supergfxctl -m Vfio
    sleep 1

    # then go back to Integrated, which powers it off again
    /usr/bin/supergfxctl -m Integrated
    ;;
esac

#!/bin/bash

# Turn off keyboard backlight before hibernate to prevent hang on power-off.
# The ASUS keyboard controller can block S4 shutdown if LEDs are active.

if [[ $1 == "pre" && $2 == "hibernate" ]]; then
  device=""
  for candidate in /sys/class/leds/*kbd_backlight*; do
    if [[ -e "$candidate" ]]; then
      device="$(basename "$candidate")"
      break
    fi
  done

  if [[ -n "$device" ]]; then
    brightnessctl -d "$device" set 0 >/dev/null 2>&1
  fi
fi

#!/bin/bash

# Lazy-unmount gvfsd-fuse filesystems before suspend/hibernate to prevent the
# kernel's process freeze from timing out. FUSE daemons (like gvfsd-fuse from
# Nautilus) can block in uninterruptible sleep during freeze, causing suspend
# to silently fail. After wake, restart gvfs so the FUSE mount is restored.

if [[ $1 == "pre" ]]; then
  while IFS=' ' read -r _ mountpoint fstype _; do
    if [[ $fstype == fuse.gvfsd-fuse ]]; then
      mountpoint=$(printf '%b' "$mountpoint")
      fusermount3 -uz "$mountpoint" 2>/dev/null || fusermount -uz "$mountpoint" 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
  done < /proc/mounts
fi

if [[ $1 == "post" ]]; then
  # Run in background — user.slice is still frozen at this point, so a
  # synchronous restart would block the thaw for up to 90 seconds.
  (
    sleep 5
    for uid_dir in /run/user/*; do
      uid=$(basename "$uid_dir")
      if [[ -S $uid_dir/bus ]]; then
        sudo -u "#$uid" env \
          DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS="unix:path=$uid_dir/bus" \
          XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$uid_dir" \
          systemctl --user restart gvfs-daemon.service 2>/dev/null || true
      fi
    done
  ) &
fi

    if [[ $2 == "hibernate" ]]; then
      /usr/bin/supergfxctl -m Vfio
      sleep 1
    fi
    ;;
  post)
    # small delay so the device is fully re-enumerated
    sleep 4

    # force-bind dGPU to vfio (fully detached from nvidia)
    /usr/bin/supergfxctl -m Vfio
    sleep 1

    # then go back to Integrated, which powers it off again
    /usr/bin/supergfxctl -m Integrated
    ;;
esac

#!/bin/bash

# Turn off keyboard backlight before hibernate to prevent hang on power-off.
# The ASUS keyboard controller can block S4 shutdown if LEDs are active.

if [[ $1 == "pre" && $2 == "hibernate" ]]; then
  device=""
  for candidate in /sys/class/leds/*kbd_backlight*; do
    if [[ -e "$candidate" ]]; then
      device="$(basename "$candidate")"
      break
    fi
  done

  if [[ -n "$device" ]]; then
    brightnessctl -d "$device" set 0 >/dev/null 2>&1
  fi
fi

#!/bin/bash

# Lazy-unmount gvfsd-fuse filesystems before suspend/hibernate to prevent the
# kernel's process freeze from timing out. FUSE daemons (like gvfsd-fuse from
# Nautilus) can block in uninterruptible sleep during freeze, causing suspend
# to silently fail. After wake, restart gvfs so the FUSE mount is restored.

if [[ $1 == "pre" ]]; then
  while IFS=' ' read -r _ mountpoint fstype _; do
    if [[ $fstype == fuse.gvfsd-fuse ]]; then
      mountpoint=$(printf '%b' "$mountpoint")
      fusermount3 -uz "$mountpoint" 2>/dev/null || fusermount -uz "$mountpoint" 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
  done < /proc/mounts
fi

if [[ $1 == "post" ]]; then
  # Run in background — user.slice is still frozen at this point, so a
  # synchronous restart would block the thaw for up to 90 seconds.
  (
    sleep 5
    for uid_dir in /run/user/*; do
      uid=$(basename "$uid_dir")
      if [[ -S $uid_dir/bus ]]; then
        sudo -u "#$uid" env \
          DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS="unix:path=$uid_dir/bus" \
          XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$uid_dir" \
          systemctl --user restart gvfs-daemon.service 2>/dev/null || true
      fi
    done
  ) &
fi

Two issues visible right away:

1. **The swayidle config still has the old version** — it has `niri msg action power-off-monitors` instead of `omarchy-brightness-display off`, and `before-sleep` is missing `OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY=true`. Looks like you edited it directly for testing but it's using the old config, not the updated one from the repo. The repo config hasn't been copied to `~/.config/swayidle/swayidle.conf` yet.

2. **`omarchy-system-lock` — the `pidof hyprlock` check is the problem.** When hyprlock is not running, it starts it in a subshell background — but then immediately continues to the `OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY` block which does `sleep 3` then checks `pidof hyprlock`. The race condition is: hyprlock takes more than 3 seconds to fully start (especially on first run), so by the time the sleep finishes, `pidof hyprlock` finds nothing and exits without turning off the display. Meanwhile hyprlock may have started but the display-off already bailed.

NAME
     swayidle - Idle manager for Wayland

SYNOPSIS
     swayidle [options] [events...]

OPTIONS
     -C <path>
	 The config file to use. By default, the following paths are checked in

	 Wait  for  command  to finish executing before continuing, helpful for

	 goes to sleep.

	 finishes.

     -S <seat-name>
	 Specify which seat to use. By default, if no name is specified, an ar‐
	 bitrary seat will be picked instead.

DESCRIPTION
     swayidle listens for idle activity on your Wayland compositor and executes
     tasks on various idle-related events. You can specify any number of events
     at the command line and in the config file.

EVENTS
     timeout <timeout> <timeout command> [resume <resume command>]
	 Execute timeout command if there is no activity for <timeout> seconds.

	 If you specify "resume <resume command>", resume command will	be  run
	 when there is activity again.

	 If  built  with  systemd support, executes command before systemd puts

	 by  the  option InhibitDelayMaxSec. A command that has not finished by

	 resume, unlock, etc.

     All commands are executed in a shell.

SIGNALS

	 Run  all  pending  resume commands. When finished swayidle will termi‐

	 bitrary seat will be picked instead.

DESCRIPTION
     swayidle listens for idle activity on your Wayland compositor and executes
     tasks on various idle-related events. You can specify any number of events
     at the command line and in the config file.

EVENTS
     timeout <timeout> <timeout command> [resume <resume command>]
	 Execute timeout command if there is no activity for <timeout> seconds.

	 If you specify "resume <resume command>", resume command will	be  run
	 when there is activity again.

     before-sleep <command>
	 If  built  with  systemd support, executes command before systemd puts
	 the computer to sleep.

	 Note: this only delays sleeping up to the limit set in	 logind.conf(5)
	 by  the  option InhibitDelayMaxSec. A command that has not finished by
	 then will continue running after resuming from sleep.

     after-resume <command>
	 If built with systemd support, executes command after	logind	signals
	 that the computer resumed from sleep.

     lock <command>
	 If  built  with  systemd support, executes command when logind signals
	 that the session should be locked

	 If built with systemd support, executes command  when	logind	signals
	 that the session should be unlocked

	 event will also cause swayidle to call SetIdleHint(false) when run, on
	 resume, unlock, etc.

     swayidle responds to the following signals:

     SIGTERM, SIGINT

	 nate.

     SIGUSR1

	      before-sleep 'swaylock -f -c 000000'

content.data:
Both issues have the same root cause — the **`before-sleep` timing**.

**Why you see your screen for 1 second before hyprlock:**

`before-sleep` fires, `omarchy-system-lock` runs, hyprlock starts as a background process (`&`). But there's a race — the system resumes from suspend/lid-open and displays come back on *before* hyprlock has rendered its first frame. So for that brief moment you see whatever was on screen before.

The fix is to make swayidle wait for hyprlock to be ready before releasing the sleep inhibitor. The man page says `-w` makes swayidle wait for commands to finish — but `omarchy-system-lock` returns immediately because hyprlock is backgrounded with `&`.

The solution is to not background hyprlock in the `before-sleep` path. Since `OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY=true` skips the display-off block, we can make hyprlock run in the foreground when called from before-sleep so swayidle's `-w` flag actually waits for it to be ready:

input.__tool_use_purpose: Fix omarchy-system-lock to run hyprlock in foreground when OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY=true so swayidle -w can wait for it
input.command: create
input.content:
#!/bin/bash

# omarchy:summary=Lock the computer and turn off the display
# omarchy:group=system
# omarchy:name=lock
# omarchy:examples=omarchy system lock

# Ensure 1password is locked
if pgrep -x "1password" >/dev/null; then
  1password --lock &
fi

if [[ ${OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY:-false} == "true" ]]; then
  # Run hyprlock in foreground so swayidle -w waits for it to be ready
  # before releasing the sleep inhibitor. This prevents the desktop from
  # being visible for a moment after waking from suspend.
  pidof hyprlock >/dev/null || hyprlock
else
  if ! pidof hyprlock >/dev/null; then
    (
      hyprlock
      omarchy-system-wake
    ) &
  fi

  (
    sleep 3
    pidof hyprlock >/dev/null || exit 0
    omarchy-brightness-keyboard off
    omarchy-brightness-display off
  ) &
fi

content.data:
Ah I misunderstood — the delay is on the **suspend path**, not idle lock. You see hyprlock appear, then there's a 3-4 second wait before the system actually suspends and screen goes off. That's coming directly from `before-sleep` and how `systemctl suspend` interacts with swayidle's `-w` flag.

Here's what happens:

1. You trigger suspend (`systemctl suspend`)
2. logind sends the sleep signal
3. swayidle intercepts it (because of `-w`), runs `before-sleep` command first
4. `omarchy-system-lock` runs hyprlock in foreground — hyprlock starts and **stays running** (it doesn't exit until you unlock)
5. swayidle is stuck waiting for hyprlock to finish because we made it foreground
6. logind has `InhibitDelayMaxSec` (default 5 seconds) — after that it forces sleep regardless

So we over-fixed the brief-desktop flash issue — running hyprlock in foreground blocks swayidle for up to 5 seconds. The fix is to use `hyprlock --immediate` or just wait until hyprlock's socket is ready rather than blocking on the process itself:

`--immediate-render` — that's exactly what we need. It tells hyprlock to draw the background immediately without waiting for resources to load. Combined with keeping hyprlock backgrounded but waiting for it to be visible, the right approach is:

Background hyprlock with `--immediate-render`, then wait just until the process exists (not until it exits), then return so swayidle releases the inhibitor quickly:

input.__tool_use_purpose: Fix omarchy-system-lock - use --immediate-render and wait only until hyprlock process is confirmed running
input.command: create
input.content:
#!/bin/bash

# omarchy:summary=Lock the computer and turn off the display
# omarchy:group=system
# omarchy:name=lock
# omarchy:examples=omarchy system lock

# Ensure 1password is locked
if pgrep -x "1password" >/dev/null; then
  1password --lock &
fi

if ! pidof hyprlock >/dev/null; then
  if [[ ${OMARCHY_LOCK_ONLY:-false} == "true" ]]; then
    # Before suspend: start hyprlock immediately and wait until it's running
    # so swayidle releases the sleep inhibitor only after lock is visible.
    # --immediate-render prevents the blank-screen flash before hyprlock renders.
    hyprlock --immediate-render &
    until pidof hyprlock >/dev/null; do sleep 0.1; done
  else
    (
      hyprlock --immediate-render
      omarchy-system-wake
    ) &

    (
      sleep 3
      pidof hyprlock >/dev/null || exit 0
      omarchy-brightness-keyboard off
      omarchy-brightness-display off
    ) &
  fi
fi

content.data:
The key line: **`Skipping screencopy`** — hyprlock on niri skips taking a screenshot of the desktop (screencopy isn't supported in this context), and uses `--immediate-render` path. Also notice **`Missing screenshot for output eDP-1`** — no desktop screenshot means it renders a blank/color background instantly.

The real issue is the **`ext_session_lock_manager_v1`** protocol. Hyprlock uses this to lock the session — the compositor (niri) only shows the lock surface after `onLockLocked` fires. Look at the last debug line: `onLockLocked called` — that's when niri actually presents the lock screen. Everything before that is setup.

The `pidof hyprlock` check returns true as soon as the process starts, but `onLockLocked` fires slightly later. We need to wait for that signal. The most reliable way without polling is a small fixed sleep after pidof confirms — just enough for the Wayland lock surface to be committed:

input.__tool_use_purpose: Fix the ready wait - sleep after pidof to give hyprlock time to commit the lock surface
input.command: strReplace
input.newStr:
# Before suspend: start hyprlock and wait until the lock surface is
    # committed to the compositor before releasing the sleep inhibitor.
    # --immediate-render draws background without waiting for resources.
    hyprlock --immediate-render &
    until pidof hyprlock >/dev/null; do sleep 0.05; done
    sleep 0.5  # Wait for ext_session_lock surface to be committed by niri
input.oldStr:
# Before suspend: start hyprlock immediately and wait until it's running
    # so swayidle releases the sleep inhibitor only after lock is visible.
    # --immediate-render prevents the blank-screen flash before hyprlock renders.
    hyprlock --immediate-render &
    until pidof hyprlock >/dev/null; do sleep 0.1; done

#!/bin/bash

# omarchy:summary=Create a desktop launcher for a terminal UI app
# omarchy:args=[name command window-style icon-url]

set -e

if (( $# != 4 )); then
  echo -e "\e[32mLet's create a TUI shortcut you can start with the app launcher.\n\e[0m"
  APP_NAME=$(gum input --prompt "Name> " --placeholder "My TUI")
  APP_EXEC=$(gum input --prompt "Launch Command> " --placeholder "lazydocker or bash -c 'dust; read -n 1 -s'")
  WINDOW_STYLE=$(gum choose --header "Window style" float tile)
  ICON_URL=$(gum input --prompt "Icon URL> " --placeholder "See https://dashboardicons.com (must use PNG or SVG!)")
else
  APP_NAME="$1"
  APP_EXEC="$2"
  WINDOW_STYLE="$3"
  ICON_URL="$4"
fi

if [[ -z $APP_NAME || -z $APP_EXEC || -z $ICON_URL ]]; then
  echo "You must set app name, app command, and icon URL!"
  exit 1
fi

ICON_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/applications/icons"
DESKTOP_FILE="$HOME/.local/share/applications/$APP_NAME.desktop"

if [[ ! $ICON_URL =~ ^https?:// ]] && [[ -f $ICON_URL ]]; then
  ICON_PATH="$ICON_URL"
else
  ICON_PATH="$ICON_DIR/$APP_NAME.png"
  mkdir -p "$ICON_DIR"
  if ! curl -sL -o "$ICON_PATH" "$ICON_URL"; then
    echo "Error: Failed to download icon."
    exit 1
  fi
fi

if [[ $WINDOW_STYLE == "float" ]]; then
  APP_CLASS="TUI.float"
else
  APP_CLASS="TUI.tile"
fi

cat >"$DESKTOP_FILE" <<EOF
[Desktop Entry]
Version=1.0
Name=$APP_NAME
Comment=$APP_NAME
Exec=xdg-terminal-exec --app-id=$APP_CLASS -e $APP_EXEC
Terminal=false
Type=Application
Icon=$ICON_PATH
StartupNotify=true
EOF

chmod +x "$DESKTOP_FILE"

if (( $# != 4 )); then
  echo -e "You can now find $APP_NAME using the app launcher (SUPER + SPACE)\n"
fi

There's the bug — **foot ignores `-e`**. It says right there: `-e: ignored (for compatibility with xterm -e)`. Foot doesn't use `-e` to run a command — it uses the positional arguments after the options directly.
